To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) cache thrashing between consecutive lookups can significantly impact the performance of stream processing applications; (2) cache thrashing can be reduced by exploiting spatial and temporal locality in the memory layout of index structures; (3) the proposed memory layout can be used in any conventional index structure, including B+ tree, R-tree, and quadtree, and can be used in conjunction with cache-conscious indexes to improve performance.

(a) conventional main memory indexes suffer from cache thrashing between consecutive accesses, which can be mitigated by exploiting the spatial and temporal locality of the accesses, and (b) our proposed index structure, which exploits spatial and temporal locality, significantly outperforms the conventional index structures, even "cache conscious" ones, on a variety of workloads, including stream processing applications.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show how to exploit cache spatial and temporal localities between consecutive lookups to improve the performance of applications.
we propose to buffer index accesses in main memory to improve performance of applications that repeatedly perform lookups on the same indexes.
we have proposed a new index organization that is designed for better utilization of cache memory, and have developed efficient algorithms for supporting index operations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need a new generation of indexes that are aware of the spatial and temporal locality that exist between lookups.
the performance of cache-conscious index structures can be significantly improved by exploiting cache locality across consecutive accesses.
the cache-conscious indexes can be made even more efficient by buffering lookups to the same cache line, thereby reducing thrashing.
